First and foremost this is a game about survival in a hostile post-apocalyptic world, the protagonist (character) versus a world that's seen many like them and seen them all die. Secondly, and this is just as important as the first, it is a game about revival; that is it's hidden goal to rebuild the world or at least tame it somewhat. Story aside, quests aside, the protagonist should be at odds with the environment almost constantly and furthermore be pushed to change it to suit their goals.

Post-apocalypse has been done time and time again, but where it truly shines is films from the 80's and early 90's that pit the "me generation" against the awful realities of a realm that simply doesn't care. Aesthetic and art styles should reflect that of the early to middle 1980's as well as general atmosphere, essentially "oldschool" cyberpunk if the world had ended rather than turned into a corporate-run dystopia. Films such as Escape from New York and Mad Max should be used for reference, novels such as The Survivalist series and the manga/anime Akira are also good sources.

Pre-war technology should in general be limited to the idealistic predictions of the millennia, but should stay away from what we have now. Advances in cybernetics and computers should head straight for robots, not for cheaper and smaller consumer devices. Devices like tablets and slim, touchscreen cellphones don't really fit, but Robocop-style augmentations complete with the characteristic 80's "futuristic" design are the goal.

Atomic power was never stigmatized and instead embraced, but the cost factor has just barely pushed it into the realm of consumer goods. Self-contained, closed-loop miniature reactors were quickly becoming the dominant powerplant in vehicles due to petroleum shortages, but were limited to the upper middle class and above in terms of cost. Obviously vehicle fleets, faced with rising fuel costs, would have turned to the minireactor as soon as they could afford it.

Likewise the military would have done the same, most military technology is on par with 1989-1995 equipment doctrine with a few exceptions. Most importantly would be the push for electromagnetic assistance for kinetic weapons, and the complete lack of diesel-powered vehicles aside from aviation and second-line equipment. (State Guard, etc) Modern conveniences like the picatinny rail are unfortunately probably not going to fit, but they're technically okay. Vehicle mechanics are intended to be a major point of the game, but aircraft likely won't have much of a use outside of world map travel.

World map and local map should be handled in the style of Fallout 2, Mount&Blade, and other games that feature a wide open world with random local maps in the terrain between the purpose-built maps for towns, cities, and special locations. Urban locations (and other worldmap features like canyons) should be partially random, with key terrain elements being a consistent feature. Likewise highways and visible roadways on the world map should follow the same rules.

Factions should have realistic relationships with both the protagonist and with other factions, this includes local gangs, settlements or towns, wider area factions, (including the protagonist's established or joined faction) and primitive factions such as tribes or intelligent mutant creatures. This is an important element that should remain a core game mechanic, and should be able to be exploited by the player through actions/questlines/etc

**Independent stories and lore**

These should be focused mainly on pre-war era, but with strict consistency with the lore. Since this is less *sci-fi* and more *alternate history* it's likely going to be best to keep stories far enough apart so they don't intersect and break things, character-driven stories a priority. (major world-changing, aka lore changing, events should be double-checked with the timeline and updated accordingly)

This is a way for others to contribute if they don't have the technical skills necessary, and for the world to balloon into something else.
